title: Transforming toxic: a new vision for urban waterways takes shape in Brooklyn – in photos
text:
Transforming toxic: a new vision for urban waterways takes shape in Brooklyn – in photos
Designers are rethinking one of New York City’s most polluted sites with climate adaptation and community benefits
The Guardian receives support for visual climate coverage from the Outrider Foundation. The Guardian’s coverage is editorially independent
Brooklyn’s Gowanus Canal, 1.8 miles long, seen on 19 August, is one of the most environmentally precarious areas in New York City. Photograph: Thalia Juarez/The Guardian
Diana Budds in New York City, with photographs by Thalia Juarez
The Gowanus Canal, a 1.8-mile waterway in Brooklyn, has long been synonymous with stench and pollution. But in recent years, it’s undergone a green transformationPhotograph: Thalia Juarez/The Guardian
For more than a century, the heavy industry concentrated along its banks – including tanneries, manufactured gas and chemical plants, and paper mills – leached mercury, lead, benzene, coal tar and other contaminants into the water, forming a 10ft-thick sludge at the bottom of the canal. The sludge seeps into the water and surrounding soil, and vaporizes into the air. In 2010, the EPA designated the Gowanus Canal a Superfund sitePhotograph: Thalia Juarez/The Guardian
Climate change is worsening some of the canal’s problems. As storms become more frequent and intense, raw sewage and untreated stormwater drain into the canal. The low-lying area’s shallow water table, along with sea level rise, can lead to flooding even when there is no rain. Two new retention tanks, both under construction, will intercept some of this wastewater and release it to the main sewer system when it can handle the volumePhotograph: Thalia Juarez/The Guardian
For more than a decade, the Gowanus Canal Conservancy (GCC), a local non-profit, has been working to reshape the canal’s watershed – a combined 1,758 acres (711 hectares) – by building green infrastructure, increasing biodiversity and improving accessibility to the waterfront through parks and open spaces. In 2017, the GCC and the landscape architecture firm Scape released a master plan for the canal’s waterfront. Much of the space will be publicly accessible thanks to a rezoning finalized in 2021, which emphasized racial and environmental justicePhotograph: Thalia Juarez/The Guardian
‘We want a rich, resilient ecosystem that supports all different kinds of plants, habitats, animal life, fish and insects,’ said Tamara Greenfield (left), deputy director of the GCC. ‘Equally important is the community. How do we engage people to be part of the vision and make sure this reflects the needs and desires of people who lived here a long time?’ ‘There was a real desire not to have new development totally sterilize or sanitize this space,’ said Gena Wirth (right) a design principal and partner at ScapePhotograph: Thalia Juarez/The Guardian
The waterfront is built to withstand occasional flooding, whether from annual king tides or a superstorm, like Sandy, said Wirth. ‘These landscapes need to age,’ she said. ‘They weren’t just about how they looked or what kind of benches they had. How do we make sure these landscapes are managing stormwater in a way that’s actually connected to the hydrology of the canal?’Photograph: Thalia Juarez/The Guardian
A section of the esplanade is furnished with picnic tables, lounge chairs and a play zone all tucked within a lush mixture of grasses, shrubs, trees and flowersPhotograph: Thalia Juarez/The Guardian
Scape built what it describes as a ‘street creek’ between two new towers, which holds and filters stormwater. It follows the path of a historic freshwater creekPhotograph: Thalia Juarez/The Guardian
The new esplanades balance stormwater management and recreation, with native plants and planters designed to withstand flooding placed along the water’s edgePhotograph: Thalia Juarez/The Guardian
‘I love that it’s not super manicured,’ says Kim Bae, a local resident. ‘This is actually why I decided to move here’Photograph: Thalia Juarez/The Guardian
Planning for a future where water access might be possible, Scape designed a stepped-down, amphitheater-like section with a gate where an access dock might goPhotograph: Thalia Juarez/The Guardian
Wirth said ecological regeneration, not restoration, guided Scape’s vision for the esplanades. ‘Restoration would aim to restore the landscape to a geographically specific prior state,’ Wirth says. ‘In our urban areas, this is often not possible or even desirable. These are new urban ecosystems with new, highly modified conditions’Photograph: Thalia Juarez/The Guardian
‘This project is about preserving the water we have, but also stepping back and designing in these more functional ecological layers,’ Wirth said. ‘A lot of people come here and they’re like: ‘Oh, is it going to be like Copenhagen, or is it going to be like Venice?’ Well, actually, it’s going to be like New York’Photograph: Thalia Juarez/The Guardian
